newsitem.title: INDONESIA: JAKARTA STOCKS DROP IN LATE TRADE ON RATES, MARGIN.
newsitem.headline: JAKARTA STOCKS DROP IN LATE TRADE ON RATES, MARGIN.

text.p: Jakarta stocks plunged 3.65 percent percent by Thursday afternoon, one of its biggest one-day falls, on accumulated worries over higher interest rates, new margin finance regulations and large rights issue payments over the next few weeks, brokers and analysts said.
The Jakarta composite index fell 25.56 points, or 3.65 percent, to 674.29 points, by 0755 GMT. Decliners led advancers by 166 to five with 17 issues unchanged.
Total turn-over was estimated at 346 billion rupiah.
The policy, however, had tightened rupiah liquidity, pushed up the rupiah interbank rate and prompted banks to increase interest rates, they said.
Keeling said some 6.74 trillion rupiah in rights issue payments over the next four weeks was part of the reason behind the fall.

This is an unprecedented amount of fund-raising by existing companies and is equivalent to 2.6 percent of the Jakarta Stock Exchange's market capitalisation of 260 trillion rupiah ($100 billion). This excluded cash demands made by new IPOs, Keeling said.
Analysts and brokers said the new margin finance regulations which limit domestic retail client leverage was also seen triggering the panic selling.
"The introduction of margin finance regulations may, if immediately and strictly enforced, cause disruption," Keeling said.
A growing proportion of retail investors are operating on margin finance.

The typical margin investor is probably 300 percent geared on the underlying cash deposit held the stockbroking company. If the client is fully invested and is faced by a rights issue, the only options are to increase leverage or sell stock, Keeling said.
Panic selling was across the board, with blue chips in the banking and property sectors suffering the most, brokers said.
Among the losers were blue chips BII, BNI and Astra
